Why Eyewitness Evidence Can Be Unreliable: Memory, Questioning, Perception, and Juror Judgment

Eyewitness evidence can seem unusually convincing because it appears to come from direct experience. If a person says they saw a suspect, watched an event happen, or remembered a key detail, a jury may treat that account as close to fact. Psychology complicates that assumption. Human memory is not a perfect recording, and perception is not the same thing as objective truth. Eyewitness evidence can be shaped by what a person expected to see, how they are questioned later, how visual evidence is interpreted, and how jurors judge confidence. This does not mean eyewitnesses are usually lying. A witness can be honest and still be wrong. Research on eyewitness testimony shows that memory, questioning, perception, and courtroom judgment all affect reliability (Granot et al., 2018; List, 1986; Peterson et al., 1999; Quigley-McBride et al., 2023).

One problem with eyewitness testimony is that memory is influenced by prior knowledge and expectations. List (1986) studied eyewitness memory for staged shoplifting events and examined age, expectations, and the type of memory test used. Participants had expectations about common and unusual objects and actions in shoplifting situations. Those expectations mattered because people do not remember events as isolated facts. They often organize events through schemas, or mental frameworks for what usually happens in a situation. A schema can make memory feel smoother and more complete, but it can also cause people to fill in missing details or remember expected information inaccurately (List, 1986).

List’s (1986) findings are important because they show that a detailed eyewitness report is not always an accurate eyewitness report. In the study, reports were more complete but less accurate for high-probability information than for low-probability information. This means people were better at producing information that fit what they expected, but some of that extra information was wrong. In a courtroom, that matters because a witness who gives many details may sound more believable. However, detail can come from expectation as well as actual memory. A witness may not be trying to mislead anyone, but the mind can still make the memory fit a familiar pattern (List, 1986).

Question wording is especially important when the eyewitness is a child. Peterson et al. (1999) studied preschool children who took part in a craft activity that included a staged accident. One week later, the children were interviewed using yes/no questions and wh- questions, such as who, what, and where questions. The study found that children’s answers changed depending on question format. Children made the most errors when answering “no” questions, and they were unlikely to say “I don’t know” when asked yes/no questions (Peterson et al., 1999).

This finding matters because yes/no questions can pressure children into giving an answer even when they are unsure. A yes/no question already contains the adult’s suggested detail. For example, a child can be asked whether someone used a broom, whether a person was wearing a hat, or whether something happened in a specific way. The child only has to accept or reject the statement. Peterson et al. (1999) found that this format can be risky because children may answer instead of admitting uncertainty. In a legal interview, that can make a weak memory sound clearer than it really is.

Wh- questions were less problematic in Peterson et al.’s (1999) study. Children were more likely to say “I don’t know” to wh- questions when they did not remember the information. That is important because an honest “I don’t know” can protect against false details. It shows the child is not just guessing or agreeing. The study does not prove that children cannot be good witnesses. Instead, it shows that adult interview methods can improve or damage the quality of a child’s testimony. A child’s reliability depends partly on how carefully the child is questioned (Peterson et al., 1999).

Eyewitness reliability also connects to visual perception. People often believe video evidence is objective because it seems to show the event directly. Granot et al. (2018) argue that this belief is too simple. Video evidence may record visual information, but people still have to interpret what they see. Attention, camera angle, vividness, and bias can shape how viewers understand a video. This means video evidence can feel more complete and neutral than it actually is (Granot et al., 2018).

Granot et al. (2018) explain that people may overbelieve video evidence. Viewers can assume their interpretation of a video is accurate and complete, even when they may have missed details or misunderstood what happened. A camera does not remove human perception from the process. It only changes where perception occurs. Instead of relying on a witness’s memory alone, the courtroom now relies on jurors’ interpretation of a visual recording. That interpretation can still be biased or incomplete (Granot et al., 2018).

Quigley-McBride et al. (2023) examined whether jurors could use information about a witness’s ability to remember faces. Face memory ability can be measured with objective tests, which may help show whether a person is generally strong or weak at recognizing faces. Across three studies, mock jurors were usually able to interpret face-memory information and combine it with confidence information. However, there was one important problem. When a witness had low confidence but a strong face-memory score, mock jurors tended to discount the witness’s uncertainty and rely too heavily on the strong face-memory score, even when expert guidance was provided (Quigley-McBride et al., 2023).

This shows that even helpful scientific information can be misunderstood. A good general ability to remember faces does not guarantee that a specific identification is accurate. A person can be good at recognizing faces and still be unsure in a particular case. Jurors may want a simple rule, such as confident means accurate or good face memory means reliable, but eyewitness evidence is more complicated than that. Accuracy depends on the original viewing conditions, the witness’s memory, the identification process, and how the evidence is explained in court (Quigley-McBride et al., 2023).

Eyewitness evidence can be useful, but it should not be treated as automatically reliable. Psychological research shows that memory can be shaped by expectations, age, and the kind of memory test used. Child witnesses can be affected by question wording, especially when adults rely on yes/no questions. Visual evidence can also be misread because video still requires human interpretation. Finally, jurors may place too much weight on confidence or misunderstand information about face-recognition ability. These problems do not mean eyewitnesses are dishonest. They mean that memory, perception, and judgment are active psychological processes. Because each process can introduce error, courts should evaluate eyewitness evidence carefully and use research-based methods to reduce mistakes.
